phonemes.desc: From √kṛ, “to do, make”; the r is syllabic-flavoured, the a long “ah”.
The abstract noun: “action”, “deed” — and by extension, the law that deeds breed consequences.

kin.label: the
kin.form: law of moral causation across all Indian traditions

pronunciation.note: The word begins as a plain noun — “deed” — and becomes the engine of the universe. The neuter gender marks the noun as a principle, not a person.

domains.title: Deed, Action, the Law of Consequence
domains.subtitle: The Engine of Moral Causation
domains.lead: Karma is the law that no deed evaporates: every act plants its seed, and the harvest is the life — and lives — that follow. From a plain Vedic noun for “ritual action” it grew into the doctrine that drives Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain cosmology alike: the moral physics by which the universe keeps its books without a bookkeeper.

cards.name: The Seed and the Fruit
cards.desc: Every deed is a seed; the fruit may ripen in this life or a later one — but it ripens.

cards.name: Action by Mind, Word, Deed
cards.desc: Karma accrues by thought, speech, and body — the three doors of action the law watches.

cards.name: The Burning Off
cards.desc: Karma can be exhausted by experience — burned like a field of stubble — or bound by attachment like a new seed.

cards.name: Liberation Beyond It
cards.desc: Mokṣa, nirvāṇa: the states beyond karma’s reach — the doctrines’ common horizon.

mythology.lead: Karma has no biography because it outranks every biography: it is the rule all biographies obey. Its ‘mythology’ is the doctrine’s own history — from the Vedic ritual’s power to bind, through the Upaniṣads’ interiorization, to the great vehicles’ global export — and the countless stories, from Nala to Savitri, in which its arithmetic drives the plot.

myths.title: From Ritual to Moral Physics
myths.text: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad relocates karma: no longer the ritual act alone but the intention behind every act — ‘one becomes good by good action, evil by evil action’. The ritual economy of the Brahmins became the moral economy of the universe, and no priest was needed to run it.

myths.title: The Owner of the Deed
myths.text: The Buddha’s formula is the doctrine’s cleanest statement: beings are the owners of their deeds, the heirs of their deeds — nowhere else does the inheritance come from. Karma in Buddhism is intention (cetanā) itself; the deed’s fruit follows like the wheel follows the ox.

myths.title: The Story Where It Breaks
myths.text: The Mahābhārata’s Savitrī tale stages the doctrine’s limit-case: Satyavān’s life exhausted by karma’s count, Yama arrives on schedule — and the wife’s flawless speech wins the husband back. The epic never denies the law; it shows a love so exact in its dharma that the law’s own keeper must honour it.

myths.title: The Subtle Dust
myths.text: Jainism made karma physical: a subtle matter that clings to the soul like dust to a wet cloth, weighing it into rebirth. The doctrine’s imagery — the soul’s lightness restored by austerity until it rises like a flame released — is the most materialist eschatology India produced.

lore.syncretism: Karma is the one doctrine shared by Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain without alteration of name — the subcontinent’s common physics. The West received it through theosophy and thence into the global vernacular, where ‘karma’ now means cosmic payback in any language; classical comparisons run to the Egyptian heart-weighing and the Greek Adrasteia.
lore.culturalLegacy: The word entered every major language as a loan — among the few Sanskrit terms to do so. It underwrites the theory of rebirth, the ethics of non-harm (the deed’s victim returns as one’s debtor), and the quietist strand of Indian political thought: the revolution you cannot make today, your karma will make eventually.
lore.extendedMeditation: Karma: the plainest noun in the batch — ‘deed’ — carrying the heaviest doctrine. Restored without marks, it reads as it acts: no ornament, no exemption, no appeal. The lexicon’s other names guard temples; this one guards the law the temples were built to honour.
lore.archaeology: Karma leaves no temple — it is the reason temples leave merit. The stūpas’ circumambulation-paths, the ghāṭs’ staircases into the rivers, and the endless charity-inscriptions of Indian epigraphy are its monuments: every recorded gift is a seed on record.
lore.cult: Its liturgy is life itself: the gift, the vow, the fast, the pilgrimage — each a karma audited at once by the doer. The śrāddha for the dead transfers merit across the ledger; the daily recitation of the deed-formulae keeps the accounts current.
lore.iconography: The wheel is karma’s emblem — the wheel of becoming, bhavacakra, held by Yama in Tibetan paintings, its hub marked by the three poisons. The ox and the cart, the seed and the sprout, the hunter’s net: the doctrine’s imagery is agricultural, mechanical, forensic.
lore.reception: The doctrine entered Western thought through Schopenhauer — who called it the finest idea humanity had produced — and through theosophy into the modern vernacular, where it now functions as secularized justice. Religious studies treat it as the most successful moral-causal theory ever devised: private, precise, and impersonal as gravity.
